\chapter{Requirement Analysis}

The objective of the requirement analysis is to establish clear expectations of the PCMA's joint design for the purposes of concept generation and development.

\section{Identification of Stakeholders}

The first step in the requirement analysis process is to identify stakeholders from the operational and support life cycle phases of the project. Stakeholders will be classified into the following categories, as defined below:
\begin{itemize}
	\item Primary stakeholders directly interact with the system while it is in operation.
	\item Secondary stakeholders contribute to the development and functioning of the system.
	\item Indirect stakeholders rely on or are affected by the system, but do not interact with the system directly.
\end{itemize}
The stakeholders relevant to the project are defined in Table~\ref{tab:SID table} below.

	\label{tab:SID table}

\section{Functional Requirements}

In this section, the primary and top-level derived functional requirements (FRs) for the joint design are defined. The only FRs that are considered are associated with joint operation. FRs are categorised into primary and derived FRs, in which:
\begin{itemize}
	\item Stakeholders are directly concerned with primary FRs.
	\item Derived FRs are required so that the system can perform primary FRs.
\end{itemize}

\section{Technical Performance Measures}

This section defines the technical performance measures (TPMs) which will be used to determine how well the joint design (NSoI) performs the required functions\footnote{TPMs are measurable and unambiguous parameters that can be influenced by designing the joint.}. The TPMs, listed in Table~\ref{tab:TPMs}, were derived from the results obtained from the generalised error-propagation model. 
\begin{table}[H]
	\centering
	\caption{Joint Technical Performance Measures}
	\label{tab:TPMs}
	\begin{tabularx}{\textwidth}{|l|X|l|l|}
		\hline
		\textbf{TPM ID} & \textbf{Related FR} & \textbf{Description} & \textbf{Target Value} \\\hline
		TPM\_01 & FR\_01, FR\_05, FR\_06, FR\_07 & Operational articulation angle & \SI{90}{\degree} \\\hline
		TPM\_02 & FR\_01, FR\_05, FR\_06, FR\_07 & Run-out tolerance & \SI{1e-3}{rad} \\\hline
		TPM\_03 & FR\_02, FR\_06, FR\_07 & Holding torque & \SI{7.725}{Nm} \\\hline
		TPM\_04 & FR\_03, FR\_04, FR\_06, FR\_07 & Encoder resolution & \SI{12}{bits} \\\hline
		TPM\_05 & FR\_01, FR\_02, FR\_05, FR\_06, FR\_07 & Joint life cycle & \num{1e6}~\text{cycles} \\\hline
	\end{tabularx}
\end{table}
The following subsections, Section 3.4.1 to 3.4.5, provide detailed calculations and mechanical justifications for TPM\_01 to TPM\_05, respectively.

\subsection{TPM\_01: Operational Articulation Angle}

The \SI{90}{\degree} articulation TPM is derived from the D-H kinematic model to ensure that the joint mechanism provides the minimum range of motion needed to cover all measurement coordinates within the PCMA working volume. This target value is a baseline of the D-H transformation chain, which guarantees that the complete kinematic path is fulfilled without restricting the arm's reach.

\subsection{TPM\_02: Run-Out Tolerance}

Minute bearing play and shaft imperfections can cause the joint to wobble during rotation. If this wobble is not bounded, it can introduce unintentional spatial drift at the probe tip. TPM\_02 ensures that the axis maintains alignment and measurement stability.

The TPM is reliant on two parameters: the nominal joint diameter, $d_{\text{joint}} = \SI{20}{mm}$, selected to match commercially available bearings, and the allowable radial bearing deflection defined under ISO 492:2014 as $\delta r_{\text{bearing}} = \SI{0.01}{mm}$ \citep{ISO492:2014}. This deflection represents the standard manufacturer precision tolerance for radial internal clearance and run-out. These parameters are used to calculate the run-out tolerance as shown in Equation~\ref{eq:TPM_02}.
\begin{equation}\label{eq:TPM_02}
	\begin{aligned}
		\Theta_{\text{runout}} &= \frac{\delta r_{\text{bearing}}}{\left(\frac{d_{\text{joint}}}{2}\right)} \\
		&= \frac{0.010}{\left(\frac{20}{2}\right)} \\
		&= \SI{1e-3}{rad}
	\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
By limiting the run-out tolerance, joint rotation only tracks single-axis motion without off-axis tilt, preserving D-H kinematic model integrity and minimising spatial errors at the probe tip.

\subsection{TPM\_03: Holding Torque}

If the position-holding mechanism is unable to produce sufficient static holding torque, the weight of the distal links can cause the arm to slip. By establishing TPM\_03, the joint is guaranteed to secure and maintain its angular position under a maximum gravity-induced cantilever moment without unexpected drift.

Figure~\ref{fig:whatsapp-image-2026-10-05-at-15} depicts the free-body diagram used to calculate the holding torque.

\begin{figure}[H]
	\centering
	\includegraphics[width=0.5\linewidth]{"../../../../../../../../../Downloads/WhatsApp Image 2026-10-05 at 15.19.12"}
	\caption{FBD of one of the Faro QuantumX links}
	\label{fig:whatsapp-image-2026-10-05-at-15}
\end{figure}

From the user manual \citep{Faro:2024}, the mass of the link is \SI{1.5}{kg}, and the distance from the center of the link to the center of the joint is \SI{0.35}{m}. The holding torque was determined using Equation~\ref{eq:holding_torque}, with a safety factor of 1.5 applied:
\begin{equation}\label{eq:holding_torque}
	\begin{aligned}
		T &= SF \cdot m \cdot g \cdot l \\
		&= (1.5)(1.5)(9.81)(0.35) \\
		&= \SI{7.725}{Nm}
	\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
By achieving this holding torque, the position-holding mechanism will successfully support the distal links when the mechanism is actuated.

\subsection{TPM\_04: Encoder Resolution}

Accurate spatial measurement in a PCMA depends on the ability of each joint's rotary encoder to digitise small angular displacements. If the optical encoder resolution is too coarse, quantisation error is emphasised, preventing the system from meeting uncertainty limits. Establishing TPM\_04 ensures that the chosen encoder resolution provides sufficient quantisation to keep measurement error minimised.

The required encoder resolution is calculated using the worst-case uncertainty established under Section 2.2, specifically $\sigma_{\theta,\text{required}} = \SI{1.957e-5}{rad}$. This value comes from the D-H kinematic error propagation derivations, applied across a full rotational range of \SI{360}{\degree}.

The minimum number of discrete pulse counts, $N_{\text{counts}}$, across a full revolution is calculated using Equation~\ref{eq:PPR_count} below.
\begin{equation}\label{eq:PPR_count}
	N_{\text{counts}} = \frac{2\pi}{\sigma_{\theta,\text{required}}} = \frac{2\pi}{1.957 \times 10^{-5}} \approx \SI{320983}{\text{CPR}}
\end{equation}
This pulse count represents the required encoder resolution to satisfy the worst-case uncertainty. This can be translated into a bit resolution as shown in Equation~\ref{eq:bit_resolution}.
\begin{equation}\label{eq:bit_resolution}
	\text{Encoder bit resolution} = \log_2(\text{CPR}) = \log_2(320\,983) \approx \SI{19}{\text{bits}}
\end{equation}
A search was conducted to obtain an encoder with the required bit resolution; however, these options were too costly considering the project budget. The highest encoder resolution obtainable within the budget was \SI{1000}{\text{PPR}}, which translates to approximately \SI{12}{\text{bits}} via quadrature decoding.

\subsection{TPM\_05: Joint Life Cycle}

By establishing TPM\_05, a baseline wear and fatigue threshold is defined to preserve long-term mechanical reliability. This will prevent joint play and measurement repeatability losses over time. Because PCMAs are passive, manually-operated systems rather than motorised, joint lifespans are not constrained by motorised duty cycles. Instead, the baseline requirement, $L_{\text{cycles}} \ge 10^6\text{ cycles}$, is established based on industry standards. This ensures that mechanical wear on critical rotating interfaces remains negligible, preserving the validity of the D-H model to ensure accuracy throughout the product's lifecycle.
